I’ve been farming these 20 mu in Quzhou for twenty years now, and I know this land well. The North China Plain gives us good soil, but water and timing are everything. Since it’s the start of the season—autumn—I’m getting ready to plant winter wheat right after I finish harvesting the summer maize stubble. I’ve got well irrigation, which is reliable, but pumping costs money and labor, so I don’t waste water. My household has four people, and some of us work off-farm, so I can’t spend all day in the fields; I need practical, efficient methods.

For the winter wheat, I’ll sow the whole 20 mu with an improved local variety—something like Jimai or Gaocheng series that my neighbors and I have trusted for years. I’ll run the rotary tiller over the maize stubble first to break it up and prepare a good seedbed. Fertilizer-wise, I’ll put down compound fertilizer at sowing and top-dress with urea in spring. Total nitrogen around 15 kg per mu, phosphorus about 6 kg, potassium about 5 kg. I’ll irrigate three times: once if the sowing bed is dry, then at green-up/jointing, and once at heading to fill the grain. I’ll spray herbicide before sowing and probably one fungicide/insecticide in spring if I see aphids or rust.

For summer maize, as soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I’ll plant hybrid seed—Zhengdan or similar—directly into the wheat stubble with minimal or no tillage to save time and catch the season. Maize needs nitrogen, so I’ll aim for about 14 kg N per mu, with 4 kg phosphorus and 4 kg potassium, applied at sowing and as a side-dress at the big-flush stage. I’ll irrigate three times: at sowing if needed, at jointing/big trumpet, and during grain filling. Two pesticide sprays should handle weeds and corn borers. I expect about 600 kg per mu for wheat and 650 kg per mu for maize if the weather cooperates.
